subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Illusory Superiority
description: A quick, practical guide to Illusory Superiority.

hook.text: 93% of American drivers rate themselves as above average. Math disagrees with all of them.

buildup.text: Svenson's 1981 study found this wasn't modesty failure. People genuinely believe they're better.

discovery.text: Illusory superiority: most people rate themselves above average on positive traits. Not everyone can be.

twist.text: The effect is strongest for skills that are hard to measure: ethics, leadership, humor, driving.

climax.text: Vague criteria let us define 'good' in ways that match our own strengths. The yardstick bends.

punchline.text: Everyone's above average in their own mirror.

quiz.question: When is illusory superiority strongest?
options: When skills are easy to measure objectively
When skills are vague and hard to measure

details.summary: Illusory superiority is the tendency for people to overestimate their own abilities relative to others. Most people rate themselves above average on driving skill, intelligence, and social ability, which is statistically impossible for the majority to be correct.
details.whyItMatters: Illusory superiority leads to underestimation of risk, rejection of helpful advice, and failure to invest in self-improvement. If you believe you are already above average, you see no need to learn, practice, or listen to criticism.
takeaways: Most people rate themselves above average on most positive traits
The bias is strongest for ambiguous or hard-to-measure skills
Overconfidence from illusory superiority increases risk-taking

faq.question: Why do most people think they are above-average drivers?
faq.answer: Driving skill is ambiguous and multidimensional. Each person defines good driving differently, emphasizing their own strengths. Someone cautious considers themselves good; someone aggressive also considers themselves skilled. Self-serving definitions enable universal overconfidence.

faq.question: Are experts immune to illusory superiority?
faq.answer: No. Experts often have stronger illusory superiority in their domain. Years of experience create overconfidence. However, experts in fields with clear feedback, like weather forecasting, show better calibration because outcomes correct their overconfidence.
